narrowest_regime: Plate counts read under FDA BAM ch. 3 (current January 2026 edition, 15-300 per plate since the March 2025 revision); QNS/hemolysis as specimen failures.
reason: The January 2026 BAM ch. 3 PDF states the suitable counting range is 15-300 per plate (updated from 25-250 in March 2025) and treats a TNTC plate as a lower bound in its maximum-likelihood APC estimate (the visible count if available, else the inhibition threshold such as 300), which is right-censoring, not missingness. A QNS specimen produces no measurement and a hemolyzed specimen is a pre-analytic rejection, so treating them as missing (not censored) is the correct distinction.

citations.cite: FDA BAM Chapter 3: Aerobic Plate Count, January 2026 edition (Zhang, Ferguson, Blodgett), fda.gov/media/191248
Haas CN, Heller B. 1988. Averaging of TNTC counts. Appl Environ Microbiol 54:2069-2072 (cited within BAM ch. 3)

bite_note: Keeping TNTC as a censored lower bound instead of dropping it as missing avoids biasing counts downward (the highest-contamination samples would otherwise be discarded); the 15 vs 25 lower bound only changes which plates are 'countable'.

narrowest_regime: Inference on a declared food exposure with structural zeros; prediction models deployed on the whole population including non-consumers.
reason: Restricting to exposure > 0 changes the target population to consumers, so any dose-response estimated is the association among consumers (varying amount given some consumption), not a whole-population effect; STROBE-nut nut-14 does require stating whether total-population or consumers-only consumption was used (nut-11 also covers handling of non-consumers). Under prediction the zeros are a valid feature value and a model trained on consumers only would be extrapolated to non-consumers at deployment, so refusing the restriction is sound given the stated premise that the model is applied to everyone.

citations.cite: Lachat C et al. 2016. Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology-Nutritional Epidemiology (STROBE-nut). PLoS Med 13:e1002036, item nut-14

bite_note: Labeling consumers-only results as an estimand change stops a consumers-only dose-response from being reported as a population effect; refusing it under prediction prevents a training/deployment population mismatch.

narrowest_regime: MS-based metabolomics where missingness rises as feature abundance falls; the signal is a likelihood, not proof, because peak-picking/alignment failures and run-day-specific LODs mix in.
reason: In MS metabolomics, missingness concentrated in low-intensity features is the textbook signature of left-censoring at a limit of detection, where whether a value is missing depends on its own unobserved value (MNAR). Wei et al. 2018 classify such values as left-censored MNAR, and Do et al. 2018 found run-day-dependent LOD missingness accounted for most missing values in a large serum dataset. The word 'likely' correctly leaves room for MCAR/MAR missingness from sample preparation or alignment.

citations.cite: Wei R et al. 2018. Missing value imputation approach for mass spectrometry-based metabolomics data. Sci Rep 8:663
Do KT et al. 2018. Characterization of missing values in untargeted MS-based metabolomics data and evaluation of missing data handling strategies. Metabolomics 14:128
Yang J et al. 2015 (presumed: A data preprocessing strategy for metabolomics to reduce the mask effect in data analysis. Front Mol Biosci 2:4); its support for this specific point not confirmed

bite_note: Classifying the pattern as left-censored sends imputation to a below-LOD method rather than a MAR method (kNN/RF), which imputes values that are too high and shrinks group differences in low-abundance metabolites. Do et al. 2018 note that kNN with variable pre-selection still performed robustly, so the downstream route deserves its own check.

narrowest_regime: Fixed-range energy/intake plausibility screens (e.g., 500-3500 kcal women, 800-4000 kcal men) on adult general-population data; weaker for Goldberg-type EI:BMR screens on FFQ data in high under-reporting populations.
reason: Fixed-range intake screens in validated adult cohorts typically exclude only a few percent of participants. A screen that would remove a majority is far more probable under a scale mismatch: kJ read as kcal is x4.184, which pushes nearly everyone over a 3500-4000 kcal cap, and a multi-day total does the same. A different reference population, such as children or athletes, also explains it. Refusing the removal until the unit is stated is a cheap, reversible guard, and 0.5 is a natural majority cut rather than a precise number. The exception is Goldberg-type under-reporting screens, where legitimate flag rates can approach or exceed half in some populations.

citations.cite: Willett W. Nutritional Epidemiology, 3rd ed. 2013 (energy plausibility ranges 500-3500 / 800-4000 kcal)
Banna JC et al. 2017. Examining plausibility of self-reported energy intake data: considerations for method selection. Front Nutr 4:45

bite_note: Without the refusal, a kJ-coded or multi-day column would cause most of the sample to be silently discarded as 'implausible'.

failing_part: "implies the covariates were measured at baseline, before the outcome"
narrowest_regime: Prospective cohorts or trials whose covariate file is the baseline visit; there the outcome name is a reasonable prior that the covariates come before the outcome, provided the user confirms it.
reason: An outcome name says when the outcome was measured, not when any covariate was measured. Common designs break the inference. Survival analyses carry time-varying or post-baseline covariates. 'Endline' and 'final' datasets are often cross-sectional surveys in which covariates are collected at the same visit as the outcome. Change-score files often hold follow-up measures beside the change. In each case a post-baseline covariate, such as a mediator or a consequence of the outcome, would be treated as a baseline confounder. At most the name raises the probability of baseline timing. No methods source supports 'implies', and the claimed basis concedes there is none.
bite_note: It moves a covariate from 'left out as another measure of the outcome' to the with-and-without adjustment pair. If that covariate was actually measured concurrently or after exposure, one arm of the pair adjusts for a mediator or collider. The user-confirmation step limits the damage only if the user notices.

failing_part: "the number of clusters minus the number of cluster-level terms (intercept, arm and any covariate constant within clusters)" as a general rule attributed to Li & Redden 2015
narrowest_regime: Two-arm CRT, GEE with a bias-corrected (KC/FG) sandwich and no covariates: t with K - 2 df, as Li & Redden 2015 evaluated.
reason: Li & Redden (2015) simulated two arms with no covariates and recommended a Wald t test with K - 2 df using the KC- or FG-corrected sandwich, which the K - 2 special case matches. They do not show that individual-level covariates cost no degrees of freedom. Much of the GEE small-sample literature instead uses K - p, with p counting all mean-model parameters. Counting only cluster-level terms is a between-within-style heuristic, plausible but not established for GEE sandwich inference. Its validity also depends on using a bias-corrected sandwich, which the claim omits.

citations.cite: Li P, Redden DT. 2015. Small sample performance of bias-corrected sandwich estimators for cluster-randomized trials with binary outcomes. Stat Med 34:281-296 (PMC4268228)
Li P, Redden DT. 2015. Comparing denominator degrees of freedom approximations for the GLMM in analyzing binary outcome in small sample CRTs. BMC Med Res Methodol 15:38 (between-within df)

bite_note: With few clusters and several individual-level covariates, K - 2 versus K - p shifts the t critical value noticeably (e.g., df 10 -> 2.228 vs df 6 -> 2.447, a ~10% wider interval), which can flip significance in small CRTs.

failing_part: "In a randomized trial the primary analysis is intention to treat" (unqualified; fails for non-inferiority/equivalence designs)
narrowest_regime: Superiority parallel or cluster-randomized trials. ITT (treatment-policy) is the standard primary analysis there, with missing outcomes handled under stated assumptions as in White et al. 2011.
reason: For superiority trials the description is correct. ITT analyses everyone as randomized, keeps the protection randomization gives, and estimates the effect of assignment, which CONSORT 2010 item 16 and White et al. 2011 support. The claim is unqualified, though. ICH E9 states that in equivalence and non-inferiority trials the full analysis set is generally not conservative, because non-adherence dilutes differences toward 'no difference'. The CONSORT non-inferiority extension therefore expects both ITT and per-protocol analyses. A further caveat: 'everyone randomized' cannot be analyzed literally when outcomes are missing without stated assumptions, and some intercurrent events such as death need a strategy other than treatment-policy.

citations.cite: Moher D et al. 2010. CONSORT 2010 explanation and elaboration. BMJ 340:c869, item 16
White IR, Horton NJ, Carpenter J, Pocock SJ. 2011. Strategy for intention to treat analysis in randomised trials with missing outcome data. BMJ 342:d40
ICH E9 (1998) Statistical principles for clinical trials, section 5.2 (full analysis set not conservative in equivalence/non-inferiority trials)
Piaggio G et al. 2012. Reporting of noninferiority and equivalence randomized trials: extension of the CONSORT 2010 statement. JAMA 308:2594-2604

bite_note: In a non-inferiority trial, an ITT-only primary analysis is biased toward declaring non-inferiority. In superiority trials the claim changes nothing relative to standard practice.

failing_part: "1.0 below 2,000 (under least squares' ... 1.5)" and "2.0 from 2,000 training rows"; the stated reason is to keep the reference journeys' picks first
narrowest_regime: Only the side remarks hold: ridge is not fit for standard inference (so a capped inference score is defensible), and with fewer than ~50 rows the CV-chosen penalty is noisy. No sample-size regime supports ranking ridge below OLS for prediction.
reason: The scores run opposite to ridge's actual advantage. Ridge with a CV-chosen penalty helps most when n is small relative to p, and its edge over OLS vanishes as n grows (Hoerl & Kennard 1970 show a positive penalty with lower MSE than OLS always exists). In simulation, test MSE/sigma^2 with p=10 was 1.345 (OLS) vs 1.222 (ridge) at n=40, falling to 1.005 vs 1.005 at n=2000. With p=30 it was 5.78 vs 1.40 at n=40, and ridge won in 70-100% of replicates below 2,000 rows. Scoring ridge below OLS under 2,000 rows and above it from 2,000 inverts this. The only reason given is to keep today's reference journeys' picks first, which is not a methods reason. The ridge-below-elastic-net ordering when p >= n holds only under sparse signals.

citations.cite: Hoerl AE, Kennard RW. 1970. Ridge regression: biased estimation for nonorthogonal problems. Technometrics 12:55-67 (existence theorem)
Zou H, Hastie T. 2005. Regularization and variable selection via the elastic net. JRSS-B 67:301-320

bite_note: In the small-n regime (n < 2,000, especially n of a few hundred or less with tens of predictors), the shelf would rank OLS above ridge. A researcher who followed it would pick the family with higher prediction error just where shrinkage matters most.

failing_part: "a deterministic fill adds no imputation uncertainty, so the intervals computed afterwards remain valid"
narrowest_regime: Only when the censored fraction is very small (roughly <=10%) does half-minimum substitution leave estimates and coverage close to nominal, and that is luck, not validity.
reason: The uncertainty about values below the LOD is real whether or not the fill represents it. A deterministic fill hides it, so the analysis treats invented values as measured. It also adds bias, because every non-detect gets one arbitrary value. Helsel (2006), the source cited, argues exactly this: substitution 'produces poor estimates of statistics', can create or hide significance, and 'should generally be considered unacceptable in scientific research'. In simulation (lognormal metabolite, group effect 0.4 on the log scale) the nominal 95% interval covered 0.857 at n=300 and 0.629 at n=1000 with 50% censoring. As an exposure, coverage was 0.839 at n=1000. Censored-likelihood (Tobit/ROS/KM) or multiple-imputation methods are the valid alternatives. A single QRILC draw is also not valid, but substitution is not the fix.

citations.cite: Helsel DR. 2006. Fabricating data: how substituting values for nondetects can ruin results, and what can be done about it. Chemosphere 65:2434-2439
Helsel DR. 2010. Much ado about next to nothing: incorporating nondetects in science. Ann Occup Hyg 54:257-262

bite_note: It approves half-minimum substitution with intervals that are too narrow and biased under heavy censoring, and it blocks the researcher from moving to a censored-data model. Coverage fell to ~63% in a realistic case.

failing_part: "not grouping by it ... is the conservative path"
narrowest_regime: None for the performance estimate. Not grouping is only harmless when the repeating column is not a unit (rows independent), and even then grouping costs little.
reason: The two errors are not symmetric. If the identifier marks real units and the folds ignore it, rows of the same unit fall on both sides of the split and the held-out score is optimistic (leakage). If it is not a real unit and the folds group by it anyway, the estimate stays roughly unbiased and slightly noisier. In simulation (80 units x 5 rows, random forest), random folds reported R2 0.60 against a true new-unit R2 of 0.31, while grouped folds reported 0.18. With independent rows, grouped and random folds gave 0.38 and 0.36 against a truth of 0.38. The conservative default under doubt is to group, as in Roberts et al. 2017. Calling not-grouping 'conservative' inverts the risk.

citations.cite: Roberts DR et al. 2017. Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography 40:913-929
Kaufman S, Rosset S, Perlich C, Stitelman O. 2012. Leakage in data mining: formulation, detection, and avoidance. ACM TKDD 6(4):15

bite_note: Whenever an unconfirmed identifier marks real units (repeat visits, patients, sites), the sealed held-out score and the CV-based model choice come out optimistic, and flexible models that memorize units get favored.

failing_part: "as efficiently as a restricted cubic spline and without its modeling assumptions, so they rank above the spline as the primary form"
narrowest_regime: None as stated. Quintiles are defensible only as a secondary, descriptive display alongside a continuous model, or when field convention requires comparability with published quintile tables.
reason: Quintiles impose a strong model: risk is flat inside each fifth and jumps at data-dependent cut points. That loses information and leaves residual confounding inside categories. The cited Royston, Altman & Sauerbrei (2006) argues against categorizing continuous predictors ('a considerable loss of power and residual confounding'), so the citation is misapplied. Bennette & Vickers (2012) make the same case for quantiles. In simulation (smooth log-shaped curve, OLS), quintile curve MSE was 1.4-5x the 4-knot spline's (e.g., 0.0080 vs 0.0016 at n=2000), and power was lower (0.23 vs 0.32 at n=500; 0.86 vs 0.94 at n=2000).

citations.cite: Royston P, Altman DG, Sauerbrei W. 2006. Dichotomizing continuous predictors in multiple regression: a bad idea. Stat Med 25:127-141
Bennette C, Vickers A. 2012. Against quantiles: categorization of continuous variables in epidemiologic research, and its discontents. BMC Med Res Methodol 12:21
Greenland S. 1995. Avoiding power loss associated with categorization and ordinal scores in dose-response and trend analysis. Epidemiology 6:450-454

bite_note: It sets the primary functional form for the main exposure, which costs power, distorts the shape (steps where the curve is smooth) and leaves within-quintile confounding in the headline estimate.

failing_part: "not the substitution curve at fixed total energy" and "[the standard model] is the route to the substitution curve"
narrowest_regime: When the true dose-response is additive in nutrient and energy (Y = h(N) + g(E)). There the residual spline is only a smoothed approximation, close at mean energy and wrong at other energies, and the standard spline recovers the fixed-energy curve. The sentence 'residual and standard models coincide only for a straight line' holds generally.
reason: With energy in the model, both specifications describe how Y changes with N at fixed total energy. They differ in structure. The standard model assumes one curve h(N) at every energy level. The residual model assumes the curve shifts along N - b(E - Ebar), and at E = Ebar its curve is exactly a fixed-energy (substitution) curve. In simulation (n=20,000, corr(N,E)=0.62, threshold-shaped curve), each model recovered the fixed-energy curve only under its own structure. Under an additive truth the RMSE was 0.056 for the standard model vs 0.113 for the residual model at mean energy, and 0.54-0.63 for the residual model at +/-1 SD of energy. Under a residual-type truth it was 0.05-0.14 for the residual model vs 0.31-0.92 for the standard model. The warning therefore states one modeling assumption as the definition of the substitution curve.

citations.cite: Willett WC, Howe GR, Kushi LH. 1997. Adjustment for total energy intake in epidemiologic studies. Am J Clin Nutr 65(4 Suppl):1220S-1228S
Tomova GD et al. 2022. Theory and performance of substitution models for estimating relative causal effects of nutritional exposures. Am J Clin Nutr 116:1379-1388

bite_note: The warning relabels a residual-scale curve and steers the researcher to the standard model. Under a residual-type truth that move gives the wrong curve shape (RMSE up to ~0.9 on a 2.6-unit range in simulation), so the decision should rest on the assumed structure or on a test of the N x E interaction, not on a definition.
